::: {.callout-tip title="Learning objectives" icon="false"}
After this lecture (and Lab 2) you can:

1. **compute** degree, closeness, betweenness, and eigenvector centrality by hand on small graphs — and **select** the right centrality for a stated question, with a justification;
2. **derive** PageRank as the fixed point of a random surfer, run two or three power iterations by hand, and explain what damping, teleport, and *personalized* PageRank each buy you;
3. **compute** clustering coefficients and explain graphlet features as a systematic subgraph census;
4. **define** modularity against its null model, step through Louvain's local-moving phase, and explain why the Laplacian's second eigenvector splits a graph;
5. **run** one round of Weisfeiler–Leman color refinement by hand and state exactly what the WL fingerprint can and cannot distinguish;
6. **build** a feature-based classifier from all of the above — and articulate why hand-crafted features hit a ceiling that no amount of engineering lifts.
:::

## The web is a graph, and importance is a fixed point

In 1998, two Stanford graduate students looked at the web the way Zachary had looked at
his karate club: as a graph whose *structure* knew something no individual page said out
loud ([Brin & Page, 1998](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0169-7552(98)00110-X)). Every hyperlink, they argued, is a tiny endorsement. But endorsements can't just be
counted — a link *from an important page* should count for more, which is circular:
importance defined in terms of importance.

::: {.predict}
**Commit before you look.** Page Q has **one** incoming link. Page V has **four**. Which
page should a search engine rank higher — or can't you tell yet?

::: {.predict-answer}
**You can't tell yet — and that is the entire idea.** If Q's single link comes from a
major hub while V's four come from pages nobody links to, Q outranks V. Counting links
is degree centrality; *weighting them by the linker's own importance* is the recursion
that made a search engine. The figure below shows exactly this happening on a toy web.
:::
:::

{{< include ../assets/figures/fig-w2-hero.html >}}

The circularity turns out to be a feature: "importance flows along links" has a unique
self-consistent solution, you can compute it by iterating a matrix product, and it is —
with refinements — what founded Google. That is today's centerpiece, and it is
**classical** graph machine learning: no training, no labels, no gradients. Pure
structure, squeezed until numbers come out.

Last week you learned to *hold* a graph. This week the graph starts talking. Everything
we extract — centralities, cluster scores, community labels, refinement colors — is a
**feature**: a number per node or per graph, computed from structure alone. Stack the
features into vectors, feed them to any classifier from your ML course, and you have
graph ML as the field practiced it for decades. At the end we will find the precise
place where this recipe stalls — which is the door the rest of the course walks through.

**Roadmap.** (1) *Who matters?* — four centralities and how to pick one. (2) PageRank:
importance as a fixed point, plus the two knobs (damping, teleport) that make it work
and the personalized variant that powers recommendations. (3) *How tight-knit?* —
triangles, clustering coefficients, graphlets. (4) *Who belongs together?* — cuts and
the Laplacian's return, then modularity and Louvain. (5) A relabeling trick from 1968
that fingerprints whole graphs — and quietly bounds what GNNs will ever see. (6) The
feature-vector recipe, and its ceiling.

::: {.callout-note title="Recap — what this lecture assumes" collapse="true"}
All from Week 1:

- The **cast graph**: nodes $A\ldots F$, edges $AB, AC, AD, BC, CE, CF, EF$, degrees $(3,2,4,1,2,2)$. It is on the board again today.
- $(\mathbf{A}^k)[u,v]$ counts length-$k$ walks ([Week 1's Proposition 1](01-why-graphs.qmd#prp-walks)) — today it counts triangles.
- The Laplacian $\mathbf{L} = \mathbf{D} - \mathbf{A}$ and its quadratic form $\mathbf{x}^\top\mathbf{L}\mathbf{x} = \sum_{(u,v)\in\mathcal{E}}(x_u - x_v)^2$. In Week 1's Q4 you showed that for an indicator vector this **counts cut edges** — hold that thought for §4.
- BFS gives shortest-path distances in unweighted graphs.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Notation for today" collapse="false"}
Every formula this week is written with the same handful of symbols; if one looks
unfamiliar mid-lecture, come back here.

- $n$ nodes and $m$ edges; the cast graph has $n = 6$ and $m = 7$.
- $d_u$ is the **degree** of node $u$; $\mathcal{N}(u)$ is its **neighbor set**; $d(u, v)$
  with two arguments is the shortest-path **distance** between $u$ and $v$ — a different
  creature despite the letter.
- $\mathbf{A}$ is the adjacency matrix, $\mathbf{D}$ the diagonal matrix of degrees,
  $\mathbf{L} = \mathbf{D} - \mathbf{A}$ the Laplacian; $\mathbf{1}$ is the all-ones
  vector and $\mathbf{I}$ the identity matrix.
- A vector of scores is written in bold, $\mathbf{x}$, and its entry for node $u$ as
  $x_u$; "$\propto$" reads "proportional to", and "$\leftarrow$" reads "is updated to".
- A sum such as $\sum_{v \in \mathcal{N}(u)} x_v$ reads "add up $x_v$ over every
  neighbor $v$ of $u$".
- A community is written $c$; $D_c$ is the sum of the degrees of its members and $e_c$
  the number of edges inside it.
:::

## 1. Who matters? Four answers before you choose one

"Which node is most important?" is not a question — it is four questions wearing one
coat. Each formalization below is a
<span class="term" data-def="Centrality: any function assigning each node a score meant to capture some notion of structural importance. There are dozens; the four here (plus PageRank) cover most real use.">**centrality**</span>,
and they genuinely disagree, so the skill worth having is not computing them (machines
do that) but *matching the definition to the question being asked*.

**Degree** $d_u$ — how many connections. On the cast graph the champion is $C$ with
$d_C = 4$. It is cheap, local, and surprisingly hard to beat as a baseline — but it sees only one
step.

**Closeness** — how near to everyone:
$$
c_{\text{clo}}(u) \;=\; \frac{n-1}{\sum_{v \neq u} d(u,v)},
$$ {#eq-w02-closeness}
where $n$ is the number of nodes and $d(u,v)$ is the shortest-path distance from $u$
to $v$ — a different creature from the degree $d_u$, despite the shared letter: in
this course $d(\cdot,\cdot)$ with two arguments always means distance. So closeness is
the inverse of $u$'s average distance to the rest. On the cast graph, from $C$ the
distances are $1,1,2,1,1$ (to $A,B,D,E,F$) — sum $6$, closeness $5/6 \approx 0.83$.
From $D$: $1,2,2,3,3$ — sum $11$, closeness $5/11 \approx 0.45$. If you are placing a
warehouse, a fire station, or a broadcast source, this is your question.

::: {.predict}
**Commit before you compute.** Does the degree champion $C$ also win on betweenness —
and who is second: $A$ (degree $3$), or one of the degree-2 nodes $B$, $E$, $F$?

::: {.predict-answer}
**$C$, with $6$; then $A$ with $4$; everyone else $0$.** Every shortest route from
$\{A,B,D\}$ to $\{E,F\}$ passes through $C$, and every route out of $D$ passes through
$A$. Degree and betweenness agree at the top here and part company beneath it: three
nodes of identical degree are, for traffic, identical zeros.
:::
:::

**Betweenness** — how often *on the way*. Take any two nodes $s$ and $t$ and ask what
fraction of their shortest routes pass through a third node $v$; add that fraction up
over every pair. A large total marks a node that many pairs cannot route around. The
formula is that sentence with the counts named:
$$
c_{\text{btw}}(v) \;=\; \sum_{\{s,t\},\, s \neq v \neq t} \frac{\sigma_{st}(v)}{\sigma_{st}},
$$ {#eq-w02-betweenness}
where the sum runs over all unordered node pairs $\{s, t\}$ avoiding $v$,
$\sigma_{st}$ counts shortest $s$–$t$ paths, and $\sigma_{st}(v)$ counts those passing
through $v$. It measures brokerage: remove a high-betweenness node and traffic reroutes
or dies. On the cast graph you can enumerate by hand: every shortest path between
$\{A,B,D\}$-side and $\{E,F\}$-side threads through $C$ — six pairs, all with a unique
shortest path — so $c_{\text{btw}}(C) = 6$; the paths from $D$ to everything except $A$
thread through $A$, giving $c_{\text{btw}}(A) = 4$; everyone else scores $0$.

**Eigenvector centrality** — important is who important people know. Score each node by
the total score of its neighbors:
$$
x_u \;\propto\; \sum_{v \in \mathcal{N}(u)} x_v
\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad
\mathbf{A}\mathbf{x} \;=\; \lambda\mathbf{x},
$$ {#eq-w02-eigvec}
where $x_u$ is node $u$'s score, $\mathcal{N}(u)$ denotes the set of $u$'s neighbors
(notation you will see weekly from now on), $\mathbf{A}$ is the adjacency matrix, and
$\lambda$ is the eigenvalue that turns the proportionality into an equality. The
importance vector is the leading eigenvector of $\mathbf{A}$, computable by repeated
multiplication (power iteration — sum your neighbors, normalize, repeat until it stops
changing). This is the recursion from the hero figure, one teleport short of PageRank.

{{< include ../assets/figures/fig-w2-cast.html >}}

::: {#exm-eig-hand .example name="Power iteration, three rounds by hand"}
**Recall** @eq-w02-eigvec: score each node by the sum of its neighbors' scores,
$\mathbf{x} \leftarrow \mathbf{A}\mathbf{x}$, then rescale and repeat until the vector
stops changing.

Start every node at score $1$ and apply "sum your neighbors" on the cast graph. One round
gives the degrees, $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{1} = (3, 2, 4, 1, 2, 2)$ for $A$ through $F$. A
second round adds up each node's neighbors' *degrees*: $A$ collects $B + C + D = 2 + 4 +
1 = 7$, $B$ collects $A + C = 7$, $C$ collects $A + B + E + F = 9$, $D$ collects $A$'s
$3$, and $E$ and $F$ each collect $C$'s $4$ plus the other's $2$, giving $6$:
$\mathbf{A}^2\mathbf{1} = (7, 7, 9, 3, 6, 6)$. A third round gives
$(19, 16, 26, 7, 15, 15)$. Scale each vector so its largest entry is $1$ and watch it
settle: after one round $(0.75, 0.50, 1, 0.25, 0.50, 0.50)$, after three
$(0.73, 0.62, 1, 0.27, 0.58, 0.58)$, and in the limit — the leading eigenvector, with
$\lambda_{\max} \approx 2.63$ — $(0.74, 0.66, 1, 0.28, 0.61, 0.61)$. $C$ leads at every
stage, but notice $B$ pulling ahead of $E$ and $F$ despite equal degrees: $B$'s two
neighbors are the two best-connected nodes in the graph, and that is exactly what the
recursion rewards.
:::

Two footnotes on the computations, for the reader who wants the machinery rather than
the library call. Betweenness looks like it needs all-pairs shortest paths, and
naively it does; the algorithm everyone uses —
[Brandes, 2001](https://doi.org/10.1080/0022250X.2001.9990249) — gets the same
numbers in $O(nm)$ by a two-pass trick per source: a BFS forward pass counts, for
every node, *how many* shortest paths from the source reach it, and a reverse pass
accumulates each node's share of the paths flowing through it (a "dependency" that
telescopes down the BFS tree). One BFS-shaped computation per source instead of one
per pair — it is the reason betweenness is computable at all on graphs of a few
hundred thousand nodes, and the reason it still is *not* at web scale, where sampled
approximations (run Brandes from a few hundred random sources) are standard.

Second footnote: between plain degree and full eigenvector centrality sits **Katz
centrality** ([Katz, 1953](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02289026)), and Week 1's
walk-counting proposition makes it transparent:
$$
\mathbf{x}_{\text{Katz}} \;=\; \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \beta^k \mathbf{A}^k \mathbf{1}
\;=\; \bigl((\mathbf{I} - \beta\mathbf{A})^{-1} - \mathbf{I}\bigr)\,\mathbf{1},
$$ {#eq-w02-katz}
where $\beta \in (0, 1/\lambda_{\max})$ is the walk discount, $\mathbf{A}^k$ counts
length-$k$ walks, $\mathbf{1}$ is the all-ones vector, $\mathbf{I}$ the identity
matrix, and $\lambda_{\max}$ is $\mathbf{A}$'s largest eigenvalue. (Fair warning:
this $\beta$ is Katz's discount; the same letter returns below with a different job,
as PageRank's damping — tradition, not identity.) In words:
"count every walk that ends at me, discounting length-$k$ walks by $\beta^k$." When $\beta$ is small the $k = 1$ term dominates and Katz is essentially degree; as
$\beta$ climbs toward $1/\lambda_{\max}$, where the series stops converging, long walks
dominate and the leading eigenvector takes over. Katz matters to us for
two reasons — it fixes eigenvector centrality's zero-score problem on directed graphs — in Katz's
original formulation every node receives a constant term before any walk is counted,
so a page with no inlinks scores that constant rather than zero, and passes it on, and its "damped walks plus a baseline"
design is one small step from the fixed point we derive next. The conceptual sequence
degree → Katz → PageRank is one dial being turned, and knowing it turns exam questions
about "compare these centralities" into recitations of a single idea.

::: {#exm-katz-hand .example name="Katz with a small discount, by hand"}
**Recall** @eq-w02-katz: $\mathbf{x}_{\text{Katz}} = \sum_{k \ge 1} \beta^{k}
\mathbf{A}^{k} \mathbf{1}$, where the $k$-th term counts the length-$k$ walks ending at
each node and $\beta^{k}$ discounts them.

Take $\beta = 0.1$ on the cast graph, well inside the safe range since
$1/\lambda_{\max} \approx 0.38$. The series starts with the walk counts you just
computed: the length-1 term is $\beta\mathbf{A}\mathbf{1} = 0.1 \cdot (3, 2, 4, 1, 2, 2)$
and the length-2 term is $\beta^2 \mathbf{A}^2\mathbf{1} = 0.01 \cdot (7, 7, 9, 3, 6, 6)$;
together they give $(0.37, 0.27, 0.49, 0.13, 0.26, 0.26)$, and every longer walk adds
only a little more, for a full sum of $(0.40, 0.29, 0.53, 0.14, 0.28, 0.28)$. Read the
ranking: it is degree's ranking with ties broken by the length-2 walks — the claim
"small $\beta$ means degree" with numbers attached. Raise $\beta$ to $0.35$, close to
the limit, and the same sum scaled to a top score of $1$ becomes
$(0.74, 0.65, 1, 0.28, 0.61, 0.61)$, which agrees with the leading eigenvector of the
example above to within a hundredth in every entry.
:::

Turn the dial yourself. The widget has one slider, $\beta$: at the left end the
ranking is degree's, in the middle Katz's, and as $\beta$ nears $1/\lambda_{\max}$ it
becomes the eigenvector's. Watch where ties break first, and find the $\beta$ past
which the order flips and stays flipped.

{{< include ../assets/d3/w2-katz.html >}}

Now stop reading definitions and *push on them* — every score below recomputes live as
you edit the graph:

{{< include ../assets/d3/w2-centrality.html >}}

The kite in the widget is a famous ten-person network built by David Krackhardt
precisely because the measures disagree on it:

{{< include ../assets/figures/fig-w2-centralities.html >}}

Diane has the most friends, but her friends all know each other — she reaches nobody new.
Fernando and Garth are closest to everyone. Heather has few connections, yet *every*
path to Ike and Jane crosses her: pure brokerage. And eigenvector centrality sides with
degree here — measures can agree, and when they do, that agreement is itself information
about the network.

The selection discipline, in one table:

| The question sounds like… | Reach for | Because it measures |
|---|---|---|
| "who has the most direct exposure?" | degree | raw connection count |
| "where do we place the depot / who spreads news fastest?" | closeness | average distance to all |
| "whose removal fragments the network / who brokers?" | betweenness | shortest-path traffic through a node |
| "who is influential among the influential?" | eigenvector / PageRank | recursive endorsement |

A warning that saves exam points and real projects: centrality scores are
*graph-relative*. A betweenness of $6$ means nothing across graphs of different sizes;
comparisons are only meaningful within one graph (or after normalization, which every
library offers and every paper forgets to state). And a habit worth forming now:
whenever a centrality drives a *decision* — who to vaccinate, which server to harden,
whose account to review — compute at least two of them and look at where they
disagree. The disagreements are not noise; they are the two definitions answering
different questions, and the disagreement set is usually where the interesting cases
live. The kite's Heather — invisible to degree, indispensable to betweenness — has a
counterpart in every real network you will ever analyze.

## 2. PageRank: importance as a fixed point

Eigenvector centrality has two cracks on directed graphs, and the web is very directed.
A page with no inlinks scores zero — and then contributes nothing to the pages it links
to, so zeros propagate. Worse, on a graph that is not strongly connected the leading
eigenvector can concentrate all mass in one corner and ignore the rest. Both cracks are
sealed by one story.

**The random surfer.** Imagine someone clicking links forever: at a page with $d^{\text{out}}_u$
outlinks they follow one uniformly at random. Define importance as *the fraction of time
the surfer spends at each page* in the long run — the
<span class="term" data-def="Stationary distribution: a probability vector r with M r = r — running the process one more step changes nothing. For PageRank's Google matrix it exists, is unique, and is what power iteration converges to.">**stationary distribution**</span>
of the walk. One bookkeeping decision first, because it is where everyone transposes
something: a *column* of the matrix answers "where does the mass at this page go
next?", a *row* answers "who sends mass to this page?". Multiplying the matrix into a
vector of page masses is then the accounting of one click — the entry for $v$
collects, from every page $u$ linking to $v$, $u$'s mass split among $u$'s outlinks.
Collect the click probabilities into the **column-stochastic** matrix
$$
M_{vu} \;=\; \begin{cases} 1/d^{\text{out}}_u & \text{if } u \to v \\ 0 & \text{otherwise,}\end{cases}
$$ {#eq-w02-M}
where $d^{\text{out}}_u$ counts $u$'s outlinks and *column-stochastic* means each
column sums to $1$ (column $u$ says where the mass at $u$ flows). Importance must
satisfy a fixed point — what flows in equals what is there:
$$
\mathbf{r} \;=\; M\mathbf{r},
$$ {#eq-w02-fixedpoint}
where $\mathbf{r}$ is the importance vector, its entry $r_u$ the surfer's long-run
visit rate at page $u$.

Read @eq-w02-fixedpoint entry by entry: on the left, the mass at a page now; on the
right, what one more click delivers there. Importance is the distribution the walk
hands back unchanged.

::: {.predict}
**Predict.** A page with no outlinks — a PDF, say — receives mass from its inlinkers
every step. Where does that mass go next, and what happens to the total $\sum_u r_u$?

::: {.predict-answer}
**Nowhere — it vanishes, and the total shrinks every step.** The page's column of $M$
is all zeros, so whatever arrives is never passed on, and on a web where every page
can reach a dead end the iteration converges to the zero vector. The mirror image —
mass entering a cycle it never leaves — is just as fatal. Both are named, and fixed,
next.
:::
:::

Two web-shaped pathologies break the plain walk. A **dead end** (page with no outlinks)
swallows mass — its column of $M$ is all zeros, so $M$ is *sub-stochastic* (some
columns sum to less than $1$), total mass shrinks every step, and
$\mathbf{r} \to \mathbf{0}$.
A **spider trap** (a cycle with no exits) collects mass forever — the walk enters and
never leaves, so the trap ends up with everything. The fix is almost comically direct:
*get bored sometimes*. With probability $\beta$ follow a link; with probability
$1-\beta$ jump to a uniformly random page:
$$
\mathbf{r} \;=\; \beta M \mathbf{r} \;+\; (1-\beta)\,\tfrac{1}{n}\mathbf{1},
$$ {#eq-w02-pagerank}
where $\beta \in (0,1)$ is the **damping factor**, $n$ the number of pages, and
$\mathbf{1}$ the all-ones vector — so the second term spreads the teleported
$(1-\beta)$ of mass evenly over all pages. The damping factor is traditionally
$0.85$ — roughly, five or six clicks
before boredom, a number chosen empirically in 1998 and never seriously dethroned. Teleporting rescues dead ends (mass reappears everywhere) and drains spider
traps (the trap leaks $1-\beta$ of its mass per step).

Watch both pathologies happen, then get fixed. Mass is drawn as the size of each
page's disc: with teleport off, a dead end drains the web toward zero and a spider
trap swallows everything; switch teleport on and watch leaked mass reappear
everywhere, the trap start bleeding, and the masses settle to one distribution
wherever you start.

{{< include ../assets/d3/w2-surfer.html >}}

::: {#def-w02-pagerank .definition name="PageRank"}
The **PageRank** of page $u$ is $r_u$, the $u$-th entry of the unique probability
vector $\mathbf{r}$ solving @eq-w02-pagerank — the stationary distribution of the
teleporting random walk. Reading guidance: it is the long-run fraction of time the
bored surfer spends at $u$; that "unique" is doing real work is exactly what the next
proposition establishes.
:::

::: {#prp-pagerank .proposition name="PageRank exists, is unique, and power iteration finds it"}
For any $0 < \beta < 1$, @eq-w02-pagerank has exactly one solution with
$\mathbf{r} \ge 0$, $\sum_u r_u = 1$, and the iteration
$$
\mathbf{r}^{(k+1)} \;=\; \beta M \mathbf{r}^{(k)} \;+\; (1-\beta)\,\tfrac{1}{n}\mathbf{1}
$$ {#eq-w02-poweriter}
converges to it from any starting distribution at rate $\beta^k$ (here
$\mathbf{r}^{(k)}$ is the estimate after $k$ updates).
:::

<details><summary>Proof (a contraction on the simplex — no Perron–Frobenius needed)</summary>
Let $G(\mathbf{r}) = \beta M\mathbf{r} + (1-\beta)\frac{1}{n}\mathbf{1}$. If
$\mathbf{r}$ is a probability vector, so is $G(\mathbf{r})$: entries are nonnegative,
and since $M$'s columns each sum to $1$, $\|M\mathbf{r}\|_1 = 1$, so
$\|G(\mathbf{r})\|_1 = \beta + (1-\beta) = 1$. For two probability vectors
$\mathbf{r}, \mathbf{s}$:
$$
\|G(\mathbf{r}) - G(\mathbf{s})\|_1 \;=\; \beta\,\|M(\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{s})\|_1 \;\le\; \beta\,\|\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{s}\|_1,
$$
because multiplying by a column-stochastic matrix cannot increase the $1$-norm (each
column redistributes its entry's mass without creating any). So $G$ is a
$\beta$-contraction on a complete space; by Banach's fixed-point theorem (any
contraction of a complete metric space has exactly one fixed point, and iterating
from anywhere reaches it) the solution
exists, is unique, and iteration converges geometrically at rate $\beta$. This is also
why large $\beta$ means slow convergence — try it in the PageRank widget later in this
section: raise $\beta$ and count the extra iterations. $\square$
</details>

The proposition licenses an algorithm — the one
[Brin & Page, 1998](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0169-7552(98)00110-X) shipped, and the
one you will write in Lab 2's exercise 1: start uniform and apply @eq-w02-poweriter
until nothing changes.

::: {#alg-w02-pagerank .algorithm name="PageRank by Power Iteration"}
Computes the PageRank vector of @eq-w02-pagerank by repeated damped updates.

**Input:** out-neighbor lists $N_{\text{out}}(\cdot)$ (an undirected edge counts in
both directions, so $|N_{\text{out}}(u)| = d_u$); damping $\beta$; iteration count $K$.
**Output:** rank vector $\mathbf{r}$ with $\sum_u r_u = 1$.

1. $n \leftarrow |\mathcal{V}|$;&nbsp; $r_u \leftarrow 1/n$ for every node $u$
2. **for** $k = 1 \ldots K$ **do**
3. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;$r'_v \leftarrow (1-\beta)/n$ for every node $v$
4. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;**for** each node $u$ **do**
5. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;$s \leftarrow \beta \, r_u \,/\, |N_{\text{out}}(u)|$
6. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;**for** each $v \in N_{\text{out}}(u)$ **do** $r'_v \leftarrow r'_v + s$
7. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;**end for**
8. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;$\mathbf{r} \leftarrow \mathbf{r}'$
9. **end for**
10. **return** $\mathbf{r}$
:::

Line 3 lays down the teleport mass; lines 4–6 push each node's retained mass
$\beta r_u$ down its outlinks in equal shares $s$. One pass of lines 3–8 is exactly
one sparse matrix–vector product, $O(m)$, and by @prp-pagerank each pass shrinks the
error by a factor $\beta$ — which is how $K$ gets chosen, as we quantify below. Lab
2's exercise 1 is this listing verbatim, checked against `networkx` to six decimals.

::: {#exm-pr-hand .example name="Two power iterations, by hand"}
**Recall** @eq-w02-poweriter: $\mathbf{r}^{(k+1)} = \beta M \mathbf{r}^{(k)} +
(1 - \beta)\tfrac{1}{n}\mathbf{1}$, where column $u$ of $M$ spreads the mass at page $u$
evenly over its outlinks (@eq-w02-M).

A three-page web: $X$ links to $Y$ and $Z$; $Y$ links back to $X$; $Z$ links to $Y$.
Take $\beta = 1$ for clean fractions (no teleport — this tiny web has no dead ends).
Columns of $M$: from $X$, half to $Y$, half to $Z$; from $Y$, all to $X$; from $Z$, all
to $Y$. Written out, with a row for each page mass *arrives at* and a column for each
page it *comes from*,
$$
M \;=\; \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 & 0 \\ \tfrac12 & 0 & 1 \\ \tfrac12 & 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix},
$$
so that in $M\mathbf{r}$ each row reads "what arrives here". Start uniform,
$\mathbf{r}^{(0)} = (\tfrac13, \tfrac13, \tfrac13)$:
$$
\mathbf{r}^{(1)} = \left(\tfrac13,\; \tfrac16 + \tfrac13,\; \tfrac16\right) = \left(\tfrac13, \tfrac12, \tfrac16\right),
\qquad
\mathbf{r}^{(2)} = \left(\tfrac12,\; \tfrac16+\tfrac16,\; \tfrac16\right) = \left(\tfrac12, \tfrac13, \tfrac16\right).
$$
The exact fixed point solves $x = y$, $y = \tfrac{x}{2} + z$, $z = \tfrac{x}{2}$:
$\mathbf{r} = (0.4, 0.4, 0.2)$. Notice $X$ and $Y$ tie even though $X$ has a single inlink and $Y$ has two:
$X$'s one inlink is $Y$'s only outlink, so it delivers all of $Y$'s mass, while
$Y$'s two inlinks bring only half of $X$'s mass plus $Z$'s smaller share. This is the midterm's favorite
computation; practice until the update is mechanical.

With teleport switched on, the update is the same routine plus one constant. At
$\beta = 0.85$ and $n = 3$ every page receives $(1 - \beta)/n = 0.05$ of teleported
mass per step, so the first step from uniform reads
$$
\mathbf{r}^{(1)} \;=\; 0.85 \cdot \left(\tfrac13, \tfrac12, \tfrac16\right) + 0.05
\;=\; (0.333,\; 0.475,\; 0.192),
$$
which still sums to $1$. Iterate and it settles at $(0.388, 0.397, 0.215)$: the
teleport has nudged a little mass toward the least-linked page $Z$ and broken the tie
between $X$ and $Y$, narrowly in $Y$'s favor.
:::

The same computation, animated, with the example's fractions beside every step. Match
each update to the one you just read; then start from $(1, 0, 0)$ and watch
$(0, \tfrac12, \tfrac12)$, then $(\tfrac12, \tfrac12, 0)$ — a different road to the
same $(0.4, 0.4, 0.2)$, which is @prp-pagerank's uniqueness in front of you.

{{< include ../assets/d3/w2-poweriter.html >}}

Three practicalities separate the formula from a deployment, and each is a known
interview question. **Dead ends, properly:** the teleport fixes their *convergence*
problem, but implementations must still decide where a dangling page's $\beta$-mass
goes each step — the standard choice redistributes it uniformly (equivalent to adding
outlinks to everywhere), and forgetting this makes rank totals drift below one, a bug
you can detect with a single `sum()` assertion (Lab 2's does). **Stopping:** the
contraction guarantees error shrinks by $\beta$ per step, so to reach tolerance
$\varepsilon$ you need $\log \varepsilon / \log \beta$ iterations — about 90 for
$\varepsilon = 10^{-6}$ at $\beta = 0.85$; note the *ranking* usually stabilizes far
earlier than the values, which matters when the ranking is all you ship.

**Scale:**
each iteration is one sparse matrix–vector product, $O(m)$ — PageRank on the full web
was, and remains, a triumph of exactly the sparse-representation discipline Week 1
preached; nobody has ever materialized the web's adjacency matrix.

**Personalized PageRank.** One word in the story is load-bearing: teleport to a
*uniformly random* page. Change the teleport distribution to a single page $q$ — or a
set of pages, say *this user's* purchases — and the whole rank distribution reorganizes
around $q$'s neighborhood. That variant, **Personalized PageRank (PPR)**, is the
workhorse of graph-based recommendation ("random walks with restarts"): importance
*relative to a viewpoint*. Same theorem, same iteration, one changed vector.

Watch all of it — convergence, damping, personalization — happen:

{{< include ../assets/d3/w2-pagerank.html >}}

PageRank will return twice: in Week 3, random-walk *embeddings* replace the fixed
teleport with learned co-occurrence statistics; and in Week 11, PPR-style diffusion is
how production systems localize a GNN's computation on billion-edge graphs.

## 3. How tight-knit? Triangles, clustering, graphlets

Centralities rank single nodes. The next family of features asks about a node's
*neighborhood texture*: are my friends friends with each other?

::: {#def-clustering .definition name="Local clustering coefficient"}
For a node $u$ with degree $d_u \ge 2$,
$$
C_u \;=\; \frac{\#\{\text{edges among } \mathcal{N}(u)\}}{\binom{d_u}{2}}
\;=\; \frac{\#\{\text{triangles at } u\}}{\binom{d_u}{2}} \;\in\; [0,1],
$$
where $\mathcal{N}(u)$ is $u$'s neighbor set and $\binom{d_u}{2}$ counts its pairs.
In words: the fraction of your friend-pairs who are themselves friends.
:::

{{< include ../assets/figures/fig-w2-cast.html >}}

On the cast graph: $C$'s neighbors are $\{A, B, E, F\}$; among the $\binom{4}{2} = 6$
pairs, exactly two are edges ($AB$ and $EF$), so $C_C = 2/6 = 1/3$. Node $A$'s
neighbors $\{B, C, D\}$ contain one edge ($BC$): $C_A = 1/3$ as well. Social networks
run high ($0.1$–$0.6$ — friends introduce friends); the web and citation graphs run much
lower; a value near the random-graph baseline $\bar d / n$ — $\bar d$ the mean degree, so
this is the chance that two random nodes are joined — is a warning that "community
structure" may be your imagination.

Where do triangle counts come from? You already own the tool:

::: {#prp-triangles .proposition name="The diagonal of A³ counts triangles"}
$$
(\mathbf{A}^3)[u,u] \;=\; 2 \times \#\{\text{triangles containing } u\},
\qquad
\operatorname{tr}(\mathbf{A}^3) \;=\; 6 \times \#\{\text{triangles in } G\},
$$ {#eq-w02-triangles}
where $\operatorname{tr}$ denotes the trace — the sum of a matrix's diagonal entries.
:::

<details><summary>Proof (two lines, standing on Week 1's shoulders)</summary>
By [Week 1's walk-counting proposition](01-why-graphs.qmd#prp-walks),
$(\mathbf{A}^3)[u,u]$ counts closed walks of length 3 at $u$.
A closed 3-walk cannot repeat a vertex (it would need a self-loop), so it is exactly a
triangle at $u$ traversed in one of its 2 orientations. The trace then counts each
triangle twice at each of its 3 vertices. $\square$
</details>

::: {.predict}
**Predict.** "The clustering coefficient of the graph" can mean two things: average
the six per-node $C_u$, or take the fraction of all *wedges* — two-edge paths — that
close into a triangle. On the cast graph, which is larger, and could the two ever
differ by more than a factor of $2$?

::: {.predict-answer}
**The per-node average, $11/18 \approx 0.61$ against $0.5$ — and yes, on heavy-tailed
graphs the gap reaches an order of magnitude.** With $D$ scored $0$ (the degree-1
convention) the local values are $\tfrac13, 1, \tfrac13, 0, 1, 1$: $B$, $E$, $F$ each
own one closed wedge and cast a full vote of $1$, while the wedge count hands $C$ six
votes, only two closed. Whoever owns the wedges wins one measure; whoever has the
head count wins the other.
:::
:::

::: {#exm-tri-hand .example name="Triangles from the matrix, by hand"}
**Recall** @eq-w02-triangles: $(\mathbf{A}^3)[u,u] = 2 \times \#\{\text{triangles
at } u\}$ and $\operatorname{tr}(\mathbf{A}^3) = 6 \times \#\{\text{triangles}\}$.

On the cast graph the diagonal of $\mathbf{A}^3$ reads $(2, 2, 4, 0, 2, 2)$ for $A$
through $F$. Halve it and you have each node's triangle count: one triangle at each of
$A$, $B$, $E$, $F$, two at $C$ (it sits in both $ABC$ and $CEF$), none at $D$. The trace
is $2 + 2 + 4 + 0 + 2 + 2 = 12 = 6 \times 2$: two triangles in the graph, each counted
six times, as @eq-w02-triangles says. Cross-check one entry against @def-clustering:
$C$'s two triangles over its $\binom{4}{2} = 6$ neighbor pairs give $C_C = 2/6$, the
value computed above.
:::

Two versions of "the graph's clustering" circulate, and they disagree often enough to
cause real confusion in papers:
$$
\bar C \;=\; \frac{1}{n}\sum_u C_u,
\qquad\qquad
T \;=\; \frac{3 \times \#\{\text{triangles}\}}{\#\{\text{wedges}\}},
$$ {#eq-w02-clustering-global}
where $C_u$ is @def-clustering's local coefficient, $n$ the number of nodes, and a
*wedge* is a path of two edges — a potential triangle. The **average clustering
coefficient** $\bar C$ gives every node one vote — so a million tight
little triangles among degree-2 nodes dominate it. The **global transitivity**
$T$ gives every wedge one vote — so hubs, who own most
wedges, dominate it. Hand-check both on the cast graph: wedges from the degree
formula, $\sum_u \binom{d_u}{2} = 3 + 1 + 6 + 0 + 1 + 1 = 12$; triangles, two ($ABC$
and $CEF$); so $T = 3 \cdot 2 / 12 = 0.5$, while $\bar C$ averages the six local values — $\tfrac13, 1, \tfrac13, 0, 1, 1$ for
$A$ through $F$, with $D$ scored $0$ by the degree-1 convention — to $11/18 \approx 0.61$. On heavy-tailed graphs the two can differ by an order of magnitude, and
"clustering coefficient = 0.6" is not a claim until you say which one. When reading
any network paper, this is the first definition to check; when writing one, state it.

Click a node in the widget: its neighbor pairs light up, the closed ones are counted,
and beside $C_u$ you see $(\mathbf{A}^3)[u,u]$ — twice the triangle count, as
@prp-triangles promised (for $C$ it reads $4$). Then switch to the two prepared
graphs, built so that $\bar C$ and $T$ disagree in opposite directions.

{{< include ../assets/d3/w2-clustering.html >}}

**Graphlets.** Triangles are one member of a family: count *all* small subgraph shapes
— the wedge, the triangle, the 4-path, the 4-star, the square, and so on — around each
node, position by position. The resulting count vector (the *graphlet degree vector*)
is a structural fingerprint far sharper than degree: two nodes can agree on degree and
clustering yet live in completely different local architectures. The price is
combinatorial: exact counts beyond 5-node graphlets are expensive, which is one reason
the next section's *iterative* fingerprint took over. In molecular graphs, graphlet-like
counts are literal chemistry — rings and motifs are function — which is why Lab 2 aims
them at protein graphs.

The widget makes "same degree, same clustering, different architecture" concrete: its
two highlighted nodes agree on both local numbers, yet their graphlet degree vectors
differ in several coordinates. Find the first coordinate that separates them — that is
the shape degree and clustering could not see.

{{< include ../assets/d3/w2-graphlets.html >}}

## 4. Who belongs together? Cuts, spectra, and modularity

Zachary's club is back, and this time we do not know the split — we want the algorithm
to *find* it. "Community" needs a definition before it needs an algorithm, and the field
settled on two families that you will now be able to derive rather than memorize.

### 4.1 The Laplacian returns: cutting where it is cheapest

In Week 1's Q4 you computed that for an indicator vector $\mathbf{x} \in \{0,1\}^n$
marking a group $S$, the quadratic form $\mathbf{x}^\top\mathbf{L}\mathbf{x}$ counts the
**cut edges** between $S$ and the rest. "Find a community" ≈ "find a cut that severs few
edges" — but *minimize the cut* alone and the optimizer cheats: cutting off a single
degree-1 node severs one edge. Real objectives (RatioCut, Normalized Cut) divide by the
group sizes to force balance, and the discrete problem promptly becomes NP-hard.

The escape is one of the prettiest moves in applied math: relax $\mathbf{x}$ from
$\{0,1\}$ labels to real numbers, and the balanced-cut problem becomes an eigenvector
problem. First, a fact that makes the smallest eigenvalues of $\mathbf{L}$ meaningful:

::: {#prp-components .proposition name="Zero eigenvalues count components"}
$\mathbf{L}$ is positive semidefinite, and the multiplicity of its eigenvalue $0$
equals the number of connected components of $G$.
:::

<details><summary>Proof (the quadratic form does all the work)</summary>
PSD: $\mathbf{x}^\top\mathbf{L}\mathbf{x} = \sum_{(u,v)\in\mathcal{E}}(x_u - x_v)^2 \ge 0$
for every $\mathbf{x}$. A vector satisfies $\mathbf{L}\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}$ iff
$\mathbf{x}^\top\mathbf{L}\mathbf{x} = 0$ (PSD makes the form's null set equal the
kernel) iff $x_u = x_v$ across every edge iff $\mathbf{x}$ is constant on each connected
component. The space of such vectors has exactly one free value per component: its
dimension is the number of components. $\square$
</details>

So on a connected graph — ordering the Laplacian's eigenvalues from smallest up,
$\lambda_1 \le \lambda_2 \le \cdots \le \lambda_n$ — we have $0 = \lambda_1 < \lambda_2$,
and the eigenvector attached to that second-smallest eigenvalue is the object this
whole subsection was built to reach.

Here is the relaxation in slow motion. A two-way split is a signal equal to $0$ on one
side and $1$ on the other, and its cut count is Week 1's quadratic form. Insisting on
two values is what makes the search combinatorial; so let every node take *any* real
number, keep the quadratic form as the thing to minimize, and add two constraints
against cheating — unit length, so the signal cannot shrink to nothing, and
orthogonality to $\mathbf{1}$, so it cannot be flat, which would be a cut that cuts
nothing. The minimizer is the eigenvector for $\lambda_2$: the smoothest signal that
is not constant.

::: {#def-w02-fiedler .definition name="Fiedler vector"}
The **Fiedler vector** of a connected graph is the eigenvector of its Laplacian
$\mathbf{L}$ for the second-smallest eigenvalue $\lambda_2$: among unit vectors
orthogonal to the constant vector $\mathbf{1}$, it minimizes the
disagreement-across-edges $\mathbf{x}^\top\mathbf{L}\mathbf{x}$. Reading guidance: it
is the *smoothest possible signal that is not constant* — the variational
characterization is proved in Week 6, where these eigenvectors become the graph's
*frequencies*.
:::

A signal
that varies as little as possible across edges but must go somewhere has one option:
sit near one value on one well-knit region, near another value on the other, and pay
its disagreement only on the thin boundary between them. Threshold it at zero and you
have cut the graph where it is cheapest.

{{< include ../assets/figures/fig-w2-cast.html >}}

::: {#exm-fiedler-hand .example name="Checking an eigenvector by hand"}
**Recall** @def-w02-fiedler: the Fiedler vector $\mathbf{v}$ satisfies
$\mathbf{L}\mathbf{v} = \lambda_2 \mathbf{v}$ with $\mathbf{L} = \mathbf{D} - \mathbf{A}$,
and entry by entry $(\mathbf{L}\mathbf{v})_u = d_u v_u - \sum_{w \in \mathcal{N}(u)} v_w$
([Week 1](01-why-graphs.qmd#eq-w01-lapaction)).

You can verify a Fiedler vector without computing one. On the cast graph
$\lambda_2 \approx 0.63$, and the widget below prints the vector, rounded, as
$(-0.26, -0.07, 0.16, -0.71, 0.44, 0.44)$ for $A$ through $F$. The entrywise formula turns each entry into a one-line check.
At the leaf $D$: $1 \cdot (-0.71) - (-0.26) = -0.45$, against
$\lambda_2 v_D = 0.63 \cdot (-0.71) = -0.45$. At $A$:
$3 \cdot (-0.26) - (-0.07 + 0.16 - 0.71) = -0.78 + 0.62 = -0.16$, against
$0.63 \cdot (-0.26) = -0.16$. Every entry passes the same test, which is what
"eigenvector" means: applying $\mathbf{L}$ only rescales it. Thresholding at zero puts
$A$, $B$, $D$ on the negative side and $C$, $E$, $F$ on the positive one — a cut of two
edges, $AC$ and $BC$. For the zero eigenvalue, take the two-piece graph (delete $CE$ and
$CF$) and the indicator of the left piece, $(1, 1, 1, 1, 0, 0)$: every node's neighbors
share its value, so every entry of $\mathbf{L}\mathbf{v}$ is $0$, and the indicator is an
eigenvector with eigenvalue $0$ — one such vector per component, as @prp-components
promised.
:::

Three small graphs first, whose spectra you can read by eye. On the two-piece graph,
count the zero eigenvalues and you have counted components, as @prp-components says;
on the cast graph and the barbell, watch $\lambda_2$ lift off zero and color each
node by the sign of its Fiedler entry — the sign boundary is the cheapest cut, and on
the barbell it is the bridge. Note where the cast graph is cut: $\{A, B, D\}$ from
$\{C, E, F\}$, for two edges — remember that partition, because §4.2's modularity
example arrives at the same one from an entirely different objective.

{{< include ../assets/d3/w2-spectral.html >}}

::: {.predict}
**Commit before you look.** One eigenvector of the karate club's Laplacian, thresholded
at zero, against the real 1977 split. Zachary's hand-built min-cut model got 33 of 34.
How many does this fully automatic spectral method get?

::: {.predict-answer}
**32 of 34.** The two misses are boundary members with ties into both camps — exactly
where a smooth signal must pass through zero. No labels, no training, no model of the
conflict: one eigenvector of a matrix you already knew.
:::
:::

{{< include ../assets/figures/fig-w2-fiedler.html >}}

For $k$ communities, take eigenvectors $2 \ldots k$ as $k{-}1$ coordinates per node and
run $k$-means (your ML course's "assign to the nearest of $k$ centroids, refit,
repeat" clustering routine) in that space — **spectral clustering**, the version you
will implement in the lab's stretch goal.

### 4.2 Modularity: communities against a null model

Spectral methods need $k$. The other family scores a *given* partition and searches for
a good one. The naive score — fraction of edges inside communities — is broken (put
everyone in one community: score $1$). The repair is a null model — in words before
symbols. For every pair the partition places together, ask: is there an edge between
them, and how much of an edge would you *expect* if every edge were rewired at random
while each node kept its degree? Sum *actual minus expected* over all such pairs. The
one-community partition now scores exactly $0$ — it collects every edge but owes the
expectation for every pair, and the two cancel. A partition scores high only when it
groups nodes connected *more than their degrees alone would predict*:

::: {#def-modularity .definition name="Modularity"}
For a partition assigning node $u$ to community $c_u$,
$$
Q \;=\; \frac{1}{2m}\sum_{u,v}\left(\mathbf{A}[u,v] - \frac{d_u d_v}{2m}\right)\delta(c_u, c_v)
\;=\; \sum_{c}\left[\frac{e_c}{m} - \left(\frac{D_c}{2m}\right)^{\!2}\right],
$$ {#eq-w02-modularity}
where $\delta(c_u, c_v)$ is the Kronecker delta — $1$ if $u$ and $v$ sit in the same
community, else $0$ — $m$ is the edge count, $e_c$ counts edges inside community $c$,
and $D_c$ sums its members' degrees. In words:
**edges observed inside, minus edges *expected* inside** if every edge were rewired at
random while preserving all degrees.
:::

The null model is the load-bearing wall. $d_u d_v / 2m$ is the expected number of edges
between $u$ and $v$ under degree-preserving random rewiring — picture cutting every
edge in half and re-splicing the $2m$ loose ends uniformly at random: a stub of $u$'s
meets a stub of $v$'s with probability $d_u d_v / 2m$-ish, and that is the baseline
$Q$ subtracts. So two hubs being connected earns a community almost no credit (hubs
connect to everyone under the null anyway), while two low-degree nodes being connected
is genuine evidence of togetherness. $Q$ ranges over
roughly $[-\tfrac12, 1)$; hand-waving calibration: real community structure typically
lands in $0.3$–$0.7$.

Watch the null model earn its name. The widget cuts every edge of the cast graph into
two stubs and re-splices the fourteen loose ends at random, over and over; pick a pair
and the frequency with which they end up joined settles toward $d_u d_v / 2m$ —
$3 \cdot 4 / 14 \approx 0.86$ for $A$ and $C$, $1 \cdot 2 / 14 \approx 0.14$ for $D$
and $E$.

{{< include ../assets/d3/w2-nullmodel.html >}}

{{< include ../assets/figures/fig-w2-cast.html >}}

::: {#exm-q-hand .example name="Modularity by hand, and a lesson"}
**Recall** @eq-w02-modularity in its community form: $Q = \sum_{c} \left[ e_c / m -
\left( D_c / 2m \right)^{2} \right]$ — edges inside each community, minus the share the
null model expects.

Cast graph, $m = 7$. Partition $\{A,B,C,D\}\,|\,\{E,F\}$: internal edges
$AB, AC, AD, BC$ and $EF$ — $e$-total $5$; degree sums $10$ and $4$. So
$Q = \tfrac{5}{7} - \left(\tfrac{10}{14}\right)^2 - \left(\tfrac{4}{14}\right)^2 \approx 0.122$.
Now move $C$ across: $\{A,B,D\}\,|\,\{C,E,F\}$ — *still* $5$ internal edges
($AB, AD$; $CE, CF, EF$), but degree sums $6$ and $8$:
$Q = \tfrac{5}{7} - \left(\tfrac{6}{14}\right)^2 - \left(\tfrac{8}{14}\right)^2 \approx 0.204$.
Same cut size, better modularity — the null model rewards taking the hub $C$ out of the
group whose expected internal edges its degree was inflating. Modularity is *not* a cut
count; it is a comparison against chance.
:::

**Maximizing Q: Louvain.** Exact maximization is NP-hard; the algorithm everyone
actually runs — from the 2008 Louvain paper
([Blondel et al., 2008](https://arxiv.org/abs/0803.0476)), one of the most-used
algorithms in all of network science — is aggressive greed in two phases. **Phase 1 (local moves):** start
with every node in its own community; sweep the nodes, moving each into the neighboring
community with the best positive $\Delta Q$, until no single move helps.
**Phase 2 (aggregation):** collapse each community into a super-node (edges become
weighted) and run phase 1 on the smaller graph. Repeat until $Q$ stops improving.

Phase 1 needs one number per candidate move: how much $Q$ changes if a node joins a
neighboring community. For the simplest case — a node that is still on its own — the
change has a closed form worth knowing by heart:

$$
\Delta Q \;=\; \frac{k_{i \to c}}{m} \;-\; \frac{D_c\, d_i}{2m^2},
$$ {#eq-w02-deltaq}

where — $i$ is the node being moved, currently in a community of its own; $c$ is the
community it is considering joining; $k_{i \to c}$ counts the edges between $i$ and the
members of $c$; $d_i$ is $i$'s degree; $D_c$ is the sum of the degrees of $c$'s
members; and $m$ is the number of edges in the whole graph. In words: the first term is
the connections $i$ actually has into $c$, as a fraction of all edges, and the second is
the connections the null model *expected* — a community with a large degree sum $D_c$
meets any node by chance, so joining it earns less credit. Louvain computes this number
for every neighboring community, takes the largest, and moves only if that largest
value is positive.

<details><summary>Where the formula comes from (two lines)</summary>
Moving an isolated node $i$ into community $c$ changes the two terms of $Q$'s community
form (@eq-w02-modularity): the internal-edge term gains $k_{i \to c}/m$, and the
expected term changes by
$-\left(\tfrac{D_c + d_i}{2m}\right)^2 + \left(\tfrac{D_c}{2m}\right)^2 + \left(\tfrac{d_i}{2m}\right)^2 = -\tfrac{D_c\, d_i}{2m^2}$,
which is @eq-w02-deltaq. For a node that already belongs to a community, Louvain first
removes it (the same formula with the sign reversed) and then inserts it, so the rule
above is the whole computation. Production implementations maintain $D_c$ and
$k_{i \to c}$ incrementally, which is how Louvain handles hundreds of millions of edges.
</details>

::: {#exm-dq-hand .example name="Three moves of phase 1, by hand"}
**Recall** @eq-w02-deltaq: $\Delta Q = k_{i \to c} / m - D_c\, d_i / 2m^{2}$, real
connections into $c$ minus the connections the null model expected.

The widget below runs on a ten-node graph with $m = 18$ edges: two dense groups,
$\{0, \ldots, 4\}$ and $\{5, \ldots, 9\}$, joined through node $4$. Follow its first
moves with a pencil; every number here reappears on the widget's panel.

*Node 0 joins node 1.* Both are alone, both have degree $3$, and they share one edge, so
$k_{i \to c} = 1$, $d_i = 3$, $D_c = 3$:
$$
\Delta Q \;=\; \frac{1}{18} - \frac{3 \cdot 3}{2 \cdot 18^2} \;=\; 0.0556 - 0.0139 \;\approx\; +0.042 .
$$
Node 0's other neighbors, nodes $2$ and $3$, have degree $4$, so joining either costs more
in the expected term: $\tfrac{1}{18} - \tfrac{12}{648} \approx +0.037$. The greedy rule
takes the largest, node $1$.

*Node 2 joins the pair $\{0, 1\}$.* Node $2$ has degree $4$ and two edges into the pair,
whose degree sum is $D_c = 3 + 3 = 6$:
$$
\Delta Q \;=\; \frac{2}{18} - \frac{6 \cdot 4}{648} \;=\; 0.1111 - 0.0370 \;\approx\; +0.074 .
$$

*Node 4, the hinge, chooses a side.* By its turn the left group is $\{0, 1, 2, 3\}$ with
$D_c = 3 + 3 + 4 + 4 = 14$, and node $4$ has two edges into it; on the right, node $5$
is still alone with degree $4$ and one edge to node $4$:
$$
\Delta Q_{\text{left}} \;=\; \frac{2}{18} - \frac{14 \cdot 4}{648} \;\approx\; +0.025,
\qquad
\Delta Q_{\text{right}} \;=\; \frac{1}{18} - \frac{4 \cdot 4}{648} \;\approx\; +0.031 .
$$
Two real edges into the left group lose to one edge into a lone node, because the left
group's degree sum has grown large enough that the null model expects node $4$ to touch
it anyway. The hinge goes right — a small, local, entirely greedy choice, and the seed of
the stall you are about to watch.
:::

Now watch the same arithmetic run. Before each move the panel under the graph prints
every option the current node is weighing, with its $\Delta Q$ from @eq-w02-deltaq; the
three calculations above are its first screens, so check your pencil against them.

{{< include ../assets/d3/w2-louvain.html >}}

The widget's stall is not a bug in the demo — it *is* the lesson. Greedy node-moves
reach a local optimum below the planted split, and the aggregation phase exists
precisely to escape such plateaus by moving whole groups at once. One caution before
you trust any $Q$: Louvain can produce internally *disconnected* communities as moves
interact; the **Leiden** algorithm
([Traag et al., 2019](https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.08473) — optional reading) repairs
this with a refinement step and is what you should reach for in production.
`networkx` ships both.

What Louvain returns on the real club is a useful surprise: *four* communities, not
two, with a $Q$ higher than the true split's. Nothing is wrong — modularity does not
know there were two leaders, only that a tighter subgroup earns more against the null
when split off. A higher $Q$ is not the same thing as the right answer.

{{< include ../assets/figures/fig-w2-louvain-karate.html >}}

Two more facts complete your modularity education. First, the objective connects back
to §4.1's spectra: [Newman, 2006](https://arxiv.org/abs/physics/0602124) showed that
maximizing $Q$ over bisections relaxes to an eigenvector problem for the **modularity
matrix**
$$
\mathbf{B}_Q \;=\; \mathbf{A} \;-\; \frac{\mathbf{d}\,\mathbf{d}^\top}{2m},
$$ {#eq-w02-modmatrix}
where $\mathbf{d}$ is the degree vector and $2m$ the total degree — observed minus
expected, entrywise: the null model as a matrix. (We subscript it $\mathbf{B}_Q$
because plain $\mathbf{B}$ was Week 1's incidence matrix, an unrelated object.) Its
*leading* eigenvector's signs propose the split, exactly as the Laplacian's *Fiedler*
eigenvector did for cuts. Two different objectives, one spectral escape hatch;
recognizing the pattern is worth more than either instance.

::: {#exm-bq-hand .example name="Three entries of the modularity matrix, by hand"}
**Recall** @eq-w02-modmatrix: $\mathbf{B}_Q[u,v] = \mathbf{A}[u,v] - d_u d_v / 2m$,
observed minus expected, one pair at a time.

On the cast graph $2m = 14$. For the pair $A, C$ — degrees $3$ and $4$, joined by an
edge — the entry is $1 - \tfrac{3 \cdot 4}{14} \approx +0.14$: an edge exists, but two
hubs meet by chance, so it earns little. For $D, E$ — degrees $1$ and $2$, not joined —
it is $0 - \tfrac{1 \cdot 2}{14} \approx -0.14$: no edge, and none was expected. For
$E, F$ — two degree-2 nodes that *are* joined — it is
$1 - \tfrac{2 \cdot 2}{14} \approx +0.71$, the strongest evidence of togetherness in the
graph, because an edge between two low-degree nodes is the one the null model least
predicts. Modularity is the sum of these entries over every pair placed in the same
community, divided by $2m$ (@eq-w02-modularity); the null-model widget above shows the
first two being earned.
:::

::: {.predict}
**Predict.** Two perfect cliques joined by a single edge. Merging them into one
community adds the bridge to the inside count — and the null model's expectation for
every pair across the two. Can the merge ever *raise* $Q$, and what decides it?

::: {.predict-answer}
**Yes — and what decides it is $m$, the size of the whole graph, not the cliques.** The
merge earns the bridge, $1/m$; it pays $D_1 D_2 / 2m^2$ for the cliques' degree sums
$D_1$, $D_2$ (the bookkeeping of @eq-w02-deltaq). Hold the cliques fixed and grow the
rest of the graph: the payment shrinks like $1/m^2$, the earning only like $1/m$, so
past some size fusing two perfect communities *improves* $Q$. The next paragraph gives
the threshold and a ring of $24$ triangles where it bites.
:::
:::

Second, the famous **resolution limit**
([Fortunato & Barthélemy, 2007](https://arxiv.org/abs/physics/0607100)), with numbers
instead of folklore. Take a ring of $c$ cliques, each of $k$ nodes ($k$ is a clique size here, not §4.1's
number of communities), joined by single
edges — an unambiguous ground truth if there ever was one. Work out the $\Delta Q$ of
merging two adjacent cliques (the exact algebra is Lab 2's stretch goal) and the
punchline is checkable: once the graph is big enough — precisely, when cliques have
fewer than $\sim\sqrt{2m}$ internal edges — the merge *increases* $Q$, and the
optimizer happily fuses perfect communities into pairs. On a ring of 24 triangles ($m = 96$),
maximum-modularity solutions merge neighbors — the ground truth is not the optimum.
Moral: $Q$ compares partitions *at a scale set by the whole graph's* $m$; small
structure is invisible to it by design, not by accident. When small communities are
the object of interest — fraud rings, protein complexes — use a resolution parameter
(both `networkx` implementations accept one) and scan it, or use methods with a
different null.

::: {#exm-ring-hand .example name="The ring of triangles, by hand"}
**Recall** @eq-w02-modularity: $Q = \sum_{c} \left[ e_c / m - \left( D_c / 2m
\right)^{2} \right]$, summed over the communities of the partition being scored.

Take $c$ triangles in a ring, each joined to the next by one edge, so $m = 4c$. Score
the honest partition, one community per triangle: each community holds $e_c = 3$
internal edges and has degree sum $D_c = 8$ (three nodes of degree $2$, two of which
carry one ring edge each), so by @eq-w02-modularity
$$
Q_{\text{truth}} \;=\; c \left[ \frac{3}{4c} - \left(\frac{8}{8c}\right)^{2} \right]
\;=\; \frac{3}{4} - \frac{1}{c}.
$$
Now merge adjacent triangles in pairs: $c/2$ communities, each with $e_c = 7$ and
$D_c = 16$,
$$
Q_{\text{pairs}} \;=\; \frac{c}{2} \left[ \frac{7}{4c} - \left(\frac{16}{8c}\right)^{2} \right]
\;=\; \frac{7}{8} - \frac{2}{c}.
$$
The merged partition wins as soon as $\tfrac{7}{8} - \tfrac{2}{c} > \tfrac{3}{4} -
\tfrac{1}{c}$, that is, for $c > 8$. At the lecture's $c = 24$ the numbers are
$Q_{\text{truth}} = 0.708$ against $Q_{\text{pairs}} = 0.792$; at $c = 6$ the truth
still wins, $0.583$ against $0.542$. Nothing about a triangle changed between the two
cases — only $m$ did.
:::

Build the ring yourself. The slider adds cliques two at a time — merged pairs need an
even count — and plots $Q$ for the ground truth, one community per clique, against $Q$
for merged adjacent pairs. For triangles the curves cross at $c = 8$; from the ninth
clique on, the wrong answer wins. Nothing about the cliques changed — only $m$ did.

{{< include ../assets/d3/w2-resolution.html >}}

## 5. The 1968 relabeling trick

Everything so far scores nodes. To classify whole graphs — is this molecule toxic? is
this binary malware? — you need features *per graph* that can be compared across graphs
of different sizes with no shared node identity. The tool the field converged on is a
relabeling procedure published by Boris Weisfeiler and Andrei Leman in 1968
([English translation](https://www.iti.zcu.cz/wl2018/pdf/wl_paper_translation.pdf) of
the original Russian article), decades
before anyone needed graph features: it was built to test
<span class="term" data-def="Graph isomorphism: a bijection between two graphs' node sets that exactly preserves edges — the graphs are 'the same drawing with different names'. No polynomial-time algorithm is known for testing it in general.">**graph isomorphism**</span>
cheaply.

**Color refinement.** Give every node the same color. Then repeat: each node's new
color is a hash of *(its color, the multiset of its neighbors' colors)* — identical
inputs, identical new color. @alg-w02-wl states the procedure exactly as Weisfeiler
and Leman conceived it, and exactly as Lab 2's exercise 5 implements it, down to the
shared signature table.

::: {#alg-w02-wl .algorithm name="Weisfeiler–Leman Color Refinement"}
Computes a color histogram per graph — comparable across graphs of any size.

**Input:** graph $G$; number of rounds $h$; signature table $T$, shared across every
graph being compared. **Output:** the histogram of all colors assigned in rounds
$0 \ldots h$ — the graph's WL fingerprint.

1. $c(v) \leftarrow c_0$ for every $v \in \mathcal{V}$ (one shared initial color)
2. **for** round $i = 1 \ldots h$ **do**
3. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;**for** each node $v$ **do**
4. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;$\mathit{sig} \leftarrow \bigl(i,\; c(v),\; \text{sorted multiset } \{c(u) : u \in \mathcal{N}(v)\}\bigr)$
5. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;**if** $\mathit{sig} \notin T$ **then** $T[\mathit{sig}] \leftarrow$ new color id
6. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;$c'(v) \leftarrow T[\mathit{sig}]$
7. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;**end for**
8. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;$c \leftarrow c'$
9. **end for**
10. **return** histogram of the colors from all rounds

:::

Three remarks on the listing. Including the round number $i$ in the signature (line 4)
keeps colors from different rounds distinct, so line 10's all-rounds histogram is well
defined. Sharing the table $T$ across graphs is what makes two fingerprints
comparable — same signature, same id, whichever graph it occurs in. And each round is
one pass over the edges, $O(m)$ with sorted buckets — $O(hm)$ total. Colors can only
split, never merge, so on $n$ nodes the refinement stabilizes within $n$ rounds.

::: {#def-w02-wl .definition name="WL fingerprint"}
The **WL fingerprint** of a graph is the histogram of colors produced by all rounds of
color refinement (@alg-w02-wl). Reading guidance: it summarizes the shape of every
node's $h$-hop neighborhood, is invariant to node renumbering, and — per @prp-wl
below — certifies difference but never sameness.
:::

{{< include ../assets/figures/fig-w2-wl.html >}}

Read the figure bottom-up: the hash table *is* the algorithm. Round 1 rediscovers
degree — but round 2 sees deeper. $B$, $E$, and $F$ all have degree 2 and share a color
after round 1; in round 2, $B$ splits away, because $B$'s neighbor-colors are
$\{1, 3\}$ (a degree-3 node and the hub) while $E$'s and $F$'s are $\{2, 3\}$ (the hub
and *each other's* class). The refinement sees *structure around* a node, not just its
degree: after $k$ rounds, a node's color encodes the shape of its entire $k$-hop
neighborhood.

{{< include ../assets/d3/w2-wl.html >}}

What is the fingerprint good for?

::: {#prp-wl .proposition name="WL is sound, not complete"}
If two graphs' WL color histograms differ at any round, the graphs are **not
isomorphic**. The converse fails: non-isomorphic graphs can share identical histograms
at every round — two triangles versus one hexagon is the smallest natural example.
:::

<details><summary>Proof sketch (one direction each)</summary>
Soundness: an isomorphism maps each node to a node with the same degree, the same
neighbor-degrees, and inductively the same color at every round — a bijection
preserving colors makes the histograms equal. So differing histograms forbid any
isomorphism. Incompleteness: in both ring graphs every node has exactly two neighbors,
and by induction every node has the same color as every other in *both* graphs at every
round (round $k{+}1$ hashes identical pairs everywhere). The histograms agree forever,
yet one graph is connected and the other is not — you just watched this in the widget's
second scene. $\square$
</details>

**From test to feature: the WL kernel.**
[Shervashidze et al., 2011](https://jmlr.org/papers/v12/shervashidze11a.html) — this
week's required reading — turned the fingerprint into machine learning: run $h$ rounds,
concatenate the color histograms of all rounds into one long count vector per graph,
and let the similarity of two graphs be the inner product of their vectors. Cost
$O(hm)$ — linear in edges — while beating the combinatorially expensive graphlet
kernels on most chemistry benchmarks. For a decade this was *the* way to classify
graphs, and it is the classifier you will build for protein graphs in the lab.

::: {#exm-wl-kernel .example name="One kernel value, by hand"}
**Recall** the kernel: run $h$ rounds of @alg-w02-wl on both graphs with one shared
signature table, count each graph's colors round by round, and let $K(G_1, G_2)$ be
the inner product of the two count vectors.

Compute one kernel value by hand, because the mechanism is simpler than the notation
suggests. Let $G_1$ be our cast graph and $G_2$ the cast graph with edge $EF$ deleted.
Round 0: both graphs are all one color — six nodes each, so the round-0 histograms
contribute $6 \times 6 = 36$ to the inner product. Round 1 refines by degree. $G_1$:
degrees $(3,2,4,1,2,2)$ → color counts $\{$deg-1: 1, deg-2: 3, deg-3: 1, deg-4: 1$\}$.
$G_2$: deleting $EF$ drops $E$ and $F$ to degree 1 → counts
$\{$deg-1: 3, deg-2: 1, deg-3: 1, deg-4: 1$\}$. Shared colors multiply:
$1{\cdot}3 + 3{\cdot}1 + 1{\cdot}1 + 1{\cdot}1 = 8$. Running total
$K(G_1, G_2) = 36 + 8 + \cdots$, with later rounds adding less and less as the
partitions diverge — while $K(G_1, G_1)$ racks up $36 + 12 + \cdots$. One deleted
edge, and the kernel already sees the two graphs drifting apart at round 1: that
sensitivity, at $O(hm)$ prices, is the entire sales pitch.
:::

Two library-shaped footnotes on the example. Real implementations hash signatures
into a shared global table so feature vectors align across a whole dataset — your
Lab 2 `wl_refine` already does this (it is @alg-w02-wl's shared $T$). And the counts
are usually normalized per graph before the SVM (support-vector machine — the
max-margin classifier from your ML course), or big molecules dominate simply by
having more nodes to count.

File one sentence away for later — arguably the most consequential sentence of the
first half of this course: **in Week 9 we will prove that message-passing GNNs
can never distinguish two graphs that WL cannot distinguish.** The 1968 trick is not
just a feature extractor — it is the ceiling of an entire architecture class you have
not met yet. When the hexagon returns, remember it fooled us honestly today.

## 6. Features into a classifier — and the ceiling

You now hold a toolbox that turns any graph into rectangles of numbers with no learning
at all:

| level | features from today | feeds |
|---|---|---|
| node | degree, closeness, betweenness, eigenvector, PageRank/PPR, clustering coefficient, graphlet degrees, community id | logistic regression, gradient boosting |
| graph | WL histogram vector, graphlet counts, size/density/degree stats | SVM with a graph kernel, gradient boosting |

The figure lays the table out as the two lanes you would actually wire up: a node lane
ending in a per-node classifier, a graph lane ending in a kernel machine. Note the one
thing they share — the graph, at the far left — and the box neither has: one where the
task may change what the features are.

{{< include ../assets/figures/fig-w2-pipeline.html >}}

This *is* a complete ML pipeline — assemble features, fit a classical model — and Lab 2
runs it three times, with a twist you should predict now. On Cora's citation graph,
seven structural *statistics* (centralities, clustering, and friends) score a dismal
≈19% against 14% chance: a paper's topic has almost nothing to do with how *important*
or *tight-knit* it is — statistics are topic-blind. Add crude *position* features — a
one-hot of the node's Louvain community — and the same classifier jumps to ≈62%,
because under homophily, topic lives in *where you sit*. That 62% is the semester's
baseline number. And on protein graphs, WL features remain close to the state of the
art *to this day* on small datasets.

The bar chart below is the semester's scoreboard; be able to say what each bar can
see. Chance, $14\%$, sees nothing; seven structural statistics, $19\%$, see how central
and clustered a paper is; the Louvain community id, $62\%$, sees *where* it sits; the
last bar, $81\%$, is Week 6's model reading graph and words together. Every big jump
admits a new *kind* of information.

{{< include ../assets/d3/w2-baseline.html >}}

So where is the ceiling? Three places, and they are structural, not fixable by more
engineering:

1. **The features are task-blind.** Betweenness does not know you are predicting paper
   topics — and the 19% above is what that blindness costs. Whatever the task actually
   needs — position in the right cluster, some pattern of co-citation, some asymmetric
   role — either survives compression into your chosen statistics or is gone before the
   classifier ever sees data. The feature designer is the bottleneck.
2. **They ignore what nodes *say*.** Cora's papers have bags-of-words; molecules have
   atom types. Today's pipeline processes structure and features in separate universes
   (concatenation at the end is a handshake, not a marriage). The whole point of
   Weeks 6–9 is machinery where structure and attributes are computed *together*.
3. **They do not improve with data.** A hundred labeled nodes or a hundred thousand —
   degree is degree. Nothing in the pipeline gets *better* by seeing more of the task.
   The defining property of representation learning, starting next week, is that the
   features themselves are what training improves.

Hold on to the baseline numbers, though. A GNN that cannot beat "logistic regression on
seven structural features" is not a deep insight — it is a bug report, and in this
course you will treat it as one.

A closing word on the word "classical", because it is often mistaken for "obsolete".
The methods of this lecture run today, at scale, in production: PageRank variants
rank far more than web pages (papers, proteins, transaction risk); Louvain/Leiden is
the workhorse inside modern LLM-retrieval systems you will meet in Week 5; WL is,
verbatim, the preprocessing step of the strongest graph-classification baselines and
— as Week 9 proves — the *ceiling* of an entire neural architecture family.

What "classical" actually means here is *cheap, interpretable, and assumption-explicit*:
you can compute these features on a laptop, explain each one to a regulator, and say
precisely which structural regularity each exploits. The deep methods coming next
trade away all three properties for adaptivity. Professionals keep both toolboxes
and know the exchange rate; that exchange rate is, in a sentence, what the rest of
this course teaches.

## Common pitfalls

::: {.callout-warning title="Pitfall 1 · Reporting 'the' centrality" icon="false"}
There is no such thing as *the* most important node — only the most important node
*under a definition*. Deliverables that say "we ranked nodes by importance" without
naming the measure and defending the match to the question are unreviewable. Say
"betweenness, because the client asked about single points of failure."
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Pitfall 2 · PageRank with β = 1 because teleport 'felt like a hack'" icon="false"}
Without teleport, dead ends leak all mass and any spider trap absorbs it: the iteration
converges to zeros or to the trap, both meaningless. The hack is the theorem: $\beta < 1$
is what makes @prp-pagerank's contraction argument work at rate $\beta$. If your ranks
are all near zero or all in one clique, check β before checking your code.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Pitfall 3 · Comparing modularity across graphs, or trusting its resolution" icon="false"}
$Q$ is calibrated against *this graph's* null model: $Q = 0.42$ on one network versus
$0.38$ on another says nothing about which is 'more clustered'. And modularity has a
**resolution limit**: on large graphs it refuses to see communities below roughly
$\sqrt{2m}$ internal edges, merging small genuine groups. If small communities matter,
scan a resolution parameter or use Leiden with a different objective.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Pitfall 4 · Reading equal WL fingerprints as 'same graph'" icon="false"}
@prp-wl is one-directional. Equal histograms mean "WL cannot tell them apart," not
"isomorphic" — the rings pair fails it, and chemistry is full of WL-equivalent
non-identical structures. In the other direction you are safe: different fingerprints
*prove* non-isomorphism.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Pitfall 5 · A fancy feature that is degree in a costume" icon="false"}
On many graphs, eigenvector centrality, PageRank, and even betweenness correlate with
degree at $0.8{+}$. Before celebrating that your feature 'predicts', check whether
plain degree predicts the same — as a control, always run the one-feature degree
baseline. (This foreshadows a Week-9 result: several published GNN gains evaporated
against properly tuned simple baselines.)
:::
